description: We are LosSolfamidas: two brothers, one at university and one in high school, at our first hackathon. We love space, video games and building things together. We made AstroGame, a browser game that teaches children aged 7–12 how astronauts stay alive on Mars with real NASA data. We bring Godot game development, well-tested code and lots of curiosity. We'd love to meet people into pixel art, sound design or teaching science to kids.
summary:
We developed AstroGame, a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12 that works as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. The player's ship has broken down on Mars: to fly home, they must find three parts to repair it while keeping the base alive sol after sol, managing power, oxygen, water, food and radiation, and sheltering from solar storms based on 8 real events from NASA's DONKI database.

It addresses the challenge by turning real mission constraints into simple game rules. Intro cards explain each resource, a "Next step" guide always shows what to do, and new challenges arrive one per sol. After each storm and at the end of the mission, the game explains cause and effect in plain language with a real NASA fact (Curiosity RAD, ISS life support, MOXIE, Opportunity).

It matters because space science is usually taught through text, while children learn best by doing. Within their first sessions, without prior knowledge, kids experience why astronauts depend on power, shielding and communication with Earth. It runs in any browser, in English and Spanish, with keyboard, gamepad or touch.
details:
WHAT IT IS

AstroGame is an isometric pixel-art survival game for children aged 7–12, made for the challenge "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer". It runs in any modern web browser (no download, no account), in English and Spanish, with keyboard and mouse, Xbox gamepad and touch controls.

HOW IT WORKS

The player is an astronaut whose ship broke down on Mars. The game runs in real time, sol by sol (a sol is a Martian day). New systems are introduced one per sol, and a "Next step" line with an on-screen arrow always shows the most urgent task. A separate Tutorial mode teaches the basics in 8 guided steps with no time pressure. The player must:

1. Manage power: batteries are physical objects, charged at the solar panels (only by day) and placed in life support, the antenna, the greenhouse and the oxygen station. One battery cannot power everything.

2. Breathe: the suit loses oxygen outside the base (faster when running). Inside, the air is breathable only while life support has power. The oxygen station refills tanks by splitting water with electricity, like the ISS.

3. Drink and eat: the astronaut gets thirsty and drinks at a dispenser. The greenhouse grows rations (lettuce, radishes and chile peppers, crops really grown on the ISS) while it has power and its crops are watered.

4. Survive solar storms: the antenna receives Earth's warning one sol before a storm (with the real Earth–Mars radio delay). The player must shelter in the Safe Room and repair the shield. Dust storms reduce solar charging and leave the panels dirty until they are cleaned.

5. Repair the ship: three parts appear on the map; installing all three wins the mission.

WHAT IT TEACHES AND WHY IT MATTERS

Every choice has a real cost: time outside costs oxygen and radiation dose, a battery can't power everything, ignoring a warning has consequences. Each sol ends with a short debrief, and the mission debrief explains what went right or wrong in simple words and adds a real NASA fact. An in-game glossary explains words like sol, radiation dose (mSv), solar storm (SEP), life support (ECLSS) and MOXIE. The goal is that children learn, by doing, how astronauts really stay alive.

REAL DATA

Solar storms use 8 real solar energetic particle events from NASA's DONKI database (2012, 2017, 2021, 2024), stored as a historical dataset with date, instrument and link (not a live feed). After each storm, a report compares the dose the player received with the dose they would have received outside, and gives the real date of the event. Radiation values and the dose limit come from Curiosity's RAD measurements and NASA-STD-3001. Facts about ISS life support and water recycling, plant growth on the ISS, MOXIE, Opportunity and the Earth–Mars communication delay come from NASA pages. As an optional background sound, players can listen to real Mars wind recorded by the SuperCam microphone on NASA's Perseverance rover. Every source is linked on the in-game "NASA data and credits" screen.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Godot Engine 4.7 (GDScript), exported to the Web and published on itch.io. The design separates simulation (systems that read and write a single game state) from presentation (HUD and menus that only listen to events). Balance numbers, real data and all texts live in data files (JSON/CSV), so teachers or the team can tune them easily. Automated headless checks validate every change (collisions, reachability of every object and behaviour tests). AI coding assistants helped write and debug code and prepare the slides; team members reviewed and play-tested every change.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Real space-weather events become game events; survival trade-offs are learned through play instead of being explained; and a step-by-step introduction plus a "Next step" guide make a complex mission accessible to young children.
